extracted.intended_audience: piano teachers, serious piano students, and professional pianists
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional and pedagogical guidelines for piano technique, practice, repertoire selection, memorization, tone production, and student-specific teaching methods aimed at developing concert-level pianists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power arises from correct technic, not special means
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no necessity for using special means to acquire power; when everything is right you will have sufficient power; you cannot help having it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power is comparative and grows from knowing the piece thoroughly and having correct technic and finger strength developed through efficient practice; do not train for power as a separate gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen weak finger joints immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak finger joints "must be made strong at once" by correct hand position and rounded, firm fingers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with hand formation away from the piano or on the keyboard; children often adapt more quickly. Use exercises to develop rounded position and nail/knuckle strength before attempting advanced repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger action is essential and must be developed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most emphatically. Finger action is an absolute essential in playing the piano. We must have finger development."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept natural unequal finger strengths; learn to adjust weight and pressure of each finger so they sound equal when desired. Teach relative natural weights and train weaker fingers to take proportionally more weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technic practice outside of pieces is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Technic practice apart from repertoire is recommended; amount varies with advancement (beginning up to four hours; later as little as one hour or short warmups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every piece is a study in technic, but separate study (scales, arpeggios, etudes) is important, especially early on. Reduce time on pure technic as facility increases, but maintain routines to keep the hand in trim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core technical elements to master
rubrics_metrics.description: Vital technical points include scales (all kinds), arpeggios, octaves, chords, pedaling, and trills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize these foundations because they constantly recur in repertoire. Treat trills as individualized problems; work endings and evenness carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not train velocity directly; it follows correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: "I never work for velocity, nor do I work _up_ velocity. That is a matter that generally takes care of itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity emerges from knowing the work, correct technic, and strong fingers; faults (weak fingers, bad touch) must be corrected first. Rapid music exposes technical faults more readily than slow music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep repertoire in repair by slow, focused practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a rotating set of pieces; identify weak spots and use slow practice with repetitions until smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to keep hundreds of pieces at performance readiness; preserve several programs and alternate. Avoid constant fast playing—slow practice permits analysis, fingering, and technical correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain technical facility with targeted exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: A few arpeggios, scales, or a brilliant etude will put the hand in condition; review first principles after breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Czerny Op. 299, Op. 740 and Chopin studies as daily technical 'bread.' If technical facility was once thoroughly acquired, it can be regained relatively quickly with focused work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study chords from the wrist with strong fingers
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best way to study chords? From the wrist and with fingers of steel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt positions for small hands (start smaller). Avoid flapping the hand or stiff high wrists; teach arm weight and finger grasp to produce a full chord tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gymnastic/massage exercises tailored to the hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Tight hands need massage to limber fingers and stretch webs; loose, flabby hands require strengthening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe gymnastic and massage work depending on the individual hand condition; technical training should render the hand flexible and strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in teaching: teach only essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: "Simplicity is the keynote of my work. I try to teach only the essentials."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit nonessential material; prioritize foundational principles that give maximum benefit. Be concise and focus on what will most effectively develop the pupil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the hand (arch and nail joint) before playing
rubrics_metrics.description: New pupils must begin with hand formation: arch of the hand and firm nail joint; do this away from piano at a table if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some advanced students must be brought back to fundamentals. The time needed depends on pupil mentality and hand type; persist until the hand holds correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive finger action policy with advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Young students need knuckle action; as nail joint becomes firmer, reduce excessive finger raising; velocity comes from less finger action, force from arm weight, lightness by withholding arm weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train intelligent fingertip movement; avoid extremes (too high or too little finger action). Adjust fingering and movement as pupil develops nail/joint control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design or select individualized technical exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors may use original exercises or select from various sources; certain principles should govern daily practice from the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include loose wrist exercises, scales, chords, and adapt exercises to pupil needs rather than rigidly following a single method book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach pedaling technique explicitly and progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: Many students misuse the damper pedal; use preparatory exercises placing heel on floor and forepart on pedal with metronome depressions, progressing from one to multiple depressions per beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train slight, controlled depressions (not full thumps) to create a 'shimmering' pedal effect; develop ankle flexibility comparable to the wrist. Illustrate with musical examples (e.g., Chopin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize rhythmic sense and interpretative result over mere technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical foundation is necessary but small compared to training rhythmic sense and producing beautiful musical interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should cultivate rhythm, imagination, and interpretative awareness (reading poetry, art, nature) to develop the pupil's musicality beyond mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat each pupil as an individual psychological study
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher must appraise capacity, intelligence, health, temperament, and adapt instruction accordingly—no two pupils should be treated the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match repertoire and method to the pupil's mentality: do not give Bach to a pupil who cannot comprehend it; avoid overwhelming or discouraging students with inappropriate material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish correct finger action at the outset (taut condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fingers should start with up movements; work toward a 'taut' condition where the finger is responsive like a fine steel spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First secure accurate single-finger up/down movements, then combine fingers to develop legato and technical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach three kinds of legato in order
rubrics_metrics.description: Three legatos: passage legato, singing legato, and accompanying legato; master passage legato first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence pedagogical goals: ensure clarity in passage legato before teaching more complex legato types for different musical functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice technic with each hand alone
rubrics_metrics.description: "I advise technic practise with each hand alone."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate-hand practice establishes independence and precision before integrating both hands; use isolation as a standard technical procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute polyphonic technic early
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach one hand to execute a different movement or touch from the other (e.g., staccato in one hand and legato in the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out scales, arpeggios, and passages with contrasting touches to develop independence and control required for polyphony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reputable technical manuals but avoid overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Heinrich Germer and Mertke are useful; work out exercises in all keys; use relatively few etudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select compact, comprehensive books to cover technical ground; supplement with teacher-created material tailored to the pupil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the metronome sparingly to build inner rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the student seems to have a very imperfect rhythmic sense, I use the metronome, but as sparingly as possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor development of internalized rhythm; reserve metronome for remediation rather than constant dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor analytic memorization when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Three memorization methods: Analytic (best), Photographic, Muscular; analytic memory picks the passage apart and learns its construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage analytical study of structure and reasons behind notes for durable memorization; allow other methods when pupil's natural tendency dictates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone color is a distinct interpretative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tone Color, as a distinct factor in musical interpretation... it is the _quality_ of tone I seek after."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on single-tone production until pupil understands desired color; use pedal judiciously (referred to as 'soul of the piano') to enhance tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select repertoire to avoid hackneyed or overly difficult works
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving pieces that are too difficult or overly familiar 'war-horses'; include lesser-known works to broaden musical exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't force pupils to struggle with a piece they will hate; instead cultivate taste and variety—teachers' individuality should reflect in repertoire choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize technic to each hand and player
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no special sort or method of technic that will do for all players... every hand is peculiar to itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and adapt methods to each hand's requirements; be flexible rather than dogmatic about a single 'method.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop technic through thought, listening, and intent practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic technic evolves from thought, hearing great music, listening to great players, and intent listening to one's own playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine mental work and listening with physical practice; cultivate musical perception alongside mechanical facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt correct point of key contact (back of tip / ball of finger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keys should not be struck with high finger action or the direct end of the finger; contact is "just back of the tip, between that and the ball of the finger."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this contact point to gain clarity and control; avoid excessive elevation of fingers which reduces clarity in rapid passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use half-staccato and pressure touches for clarity and color
rubrics_metrics.description: Legato alone sometimes lacks clarity in rapid passages; half-staccato produces a 'string of pearls' effect; use pressure/caressing touch to shape tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a variety of touches (half-staccato, pressure) to achieve brilliance and clarity rather than relying solely on legato.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ weight touch and whole-body resonance for tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight touch uses arms, shoulders, and the whole body "feels and vibrates with the tones of the piano."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate arm and body weight into tone production while coordinating with finger action for varied dynamics and colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorization via deep concentration and mental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some players memorize without a set method by periods of deep concentration and intent listening; mental study complements physical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do mental rehearsal and detailed analysis; for concertos, understand orchestral parts as well as piano part to maintain ensemble awareness in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert difficult passages into technical exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Make technical exercises out of knotty sections, sometimes playing them in many varied ways until mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devote focused, possibly intense daily sessions to specific problematic passages (examples: multiple repetitions, forty to fifty different treatments) to ensure permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance daily practice time with mental preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: An hour's actual playing may be sufficient to prepare for a recital if combined with serious mental work; some artists nonetheless practice many hours (e.g., six hours/day) when preparing new programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt practice duration to circumstances—sustained intense study during program preparation, and focused shorter physical sessions supplemented by mental rehearsal for performance readiness.
